## Introduction

- Total pancreatectomy is associated with **significant metabolic consequences** secondary to the loss of exocrine and endocrine function.
- Resultant **brittle type III diabetes** can be difficult to manage and result in severe recurrent hypoglycemia in some patients.
- Outcomes after total pancreatectomy for **pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PDAC)** are particularly poor, and this operation is **rarely indicated** in this setting.
- More appropriate indications include:
    - Chronic pancreatitis
    - Recurrent acute pancreatitis
    - Hereditary pancreatitis
    - Main-duct intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN) involving the entire gland
- **Islet auto transplant** is offered at select centers and may be considered, particularly for benign disease.
- With advances in pancreatic enzyme supplementation and insulin management, total pancreatectomy can be performed safely with acceptable quality of life in appropriately selected patients.

## Metabolic Consequences of Total Pancreatectomy

- **Complete loss of exocrine function** → malabsorption, steatorrhea, need for lifelong pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy
- **Complete loss of endocrine function** → brittle type IIIc diabetes
    - Loss of both insulin-producing β-cells and glucagon-producing α-cells
    - Severe recurrent hypoglycemia is a major risk
- Difficult to manage; requires close endocrinology follow-up
- Quality of life considerations must be discussed extensively with patients preoperatively
- These consequences underscore the need for careful patient selection

## Indications — Overview

- Total pancreatectomy is reserved for specific clinical scenarios where lesser resections are inadequate
- The operation is **rarely indicated for pancreatic adenocarcinoma** due to poor outcomes
- Best outcomes are seen in **benign and premalignant disease**
- Islet auto transplantation should be considered whenever feasible, particularly for benign indications
- Patient selection and thorough preoperative counseling are paramount

## Box 117C.1: Indications — Benign

| Indication | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Chronic pancreatitis** | After exhausting other options |
| **Recurrent acute pancreatitis** | After exhausting other options |
| **Hereditary pancreatitis** | Prophylactic and therapeutic rationale |

- Benign indications are the most common and best-supported reasons for total pancreatectomy
- Surgery is considered only after other medical, endoscopic, and surgical options have been exhausted

## Box 117C.1: Indications — Premalignant

| Indication | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN)** | With inability to clear margin |

- IPMN represents a **field defect** — the entire gland may be at risk
- Diffuse main-duct involvement or multifocal high-grade dysplasia may necessitate total pancreatectomy
- Patients should be counseled preoperatively about the possibility of completion pancreatectomy if margins cannot be cleared

## Box 117C.1: Indications — Malignant

| Indication | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Pancreatic adenocarcinoma** | With inability to clear margin (rarely, after careful consideration) |
| **Completion pancreatectomy** | For new/recurrent premalignant or malignant neoplasm |
| **Completion pancreatectomy** | For uncontrolled pancreatic leak after partial pancreatectomy after exhausting other options (extremely rare) |

- Malignant indications are uncommon due to poor survival outcomes
- Completion pancreatectomy for adenocarcinoma at the resection margin remains controversial

## Preparation — Overview

- **Proper preoperative planning is the backbone for success**
- Appropriate cardiopulmonary and medical work-up is essential
- **Extensive counseling** regarding the endocrine and exocrine consequences of total pancreatectomy is necessary
- The patient should be followed closely by the **endocrinology team** in the perioperative period
- **Indications and goals of surgery** must be discussed extensively to ensure the patient is able to make an informed decision
- Discussion is tailored to indication and varies considerably between benign and malignant processes
- **Auto islet cell transplantation** is gaining acceptance and should also be considered, particularly for patients with benign disease

## Box 117C.2: Preoperative Checklist

| Item |
|---|
| Goals of surgery discussion |
| Endocrinology evaluation |
| Postsplenectomy vaccines |
| Consideration of auto islet cell transplantation if appropriate |
| Consideration of diagnostic laparoscopy for malignant disease |
| Preoperative antibiotics |
| Thromboembolism prophylaxis |

- This checklist ensures all critical preoperative steps are addressed before proceeding to the operating room

## Preparation — Morning of Surgery

- **Thoracic epidural** placed for analgesia
- **Arterial line** placed for hemodynamic monitoring
- **Foley catheter** placed for urine output monitoring
- **Radiology images** displayed and reviewed
- A **single preoperative dose of antibiotics** administered
- A **prophylactic dose of heparin** administered
- **Sequential compression devices** placed on bilateral lower extremities
- A **hard-stop time out** is performed before incision

## Positioning, Incision, and Exposure

- Patient positioned **supine** with arms at 90 degrees (or tucked at the side)
- Careful attention to **padding all pressure points**
- Abdomen **prepped widely**
- **Diagnostic laparoscopy** performed if indicated
- In most cases, a **midline incision** provides adequate exposure
- Some surgeons prefer a **bilateral subcostal incision**
- Abdominal cavity **carefully inspected** to ensure no benign or malignant processes preclude resection
- A **self-retaining retractor** is used to gain exposure to the entire peritoneal cavity

## Exposure — Key Surgical Considerations

- The resection portion combines techniques previously discussed for:
    - **Pancreaticoduodenectomy (PD)** — Chapter 117A
    - **Distal pancreatectomy** — Chapter 117B
- Patients with **chronic and recurrent acute pancreatitis** often have a particularly **hostile operative field**
- The surgeon must have significant experience operating in this setting
- Dense inflammatory and adhesions are common and require meticulous dissection

## Kocher Maneuver and Entry of the Lesser Sac

- Resection begins with a **generous Kocher maneuver** to expose the **left renal vein** and **aorta**
- The **hepatic flexure** is mobilized
- The **omentum** is dissected free from the transverse colon
- The **lesser sac** is carefully inspected
- The attachments between the **pancreas and stomach** are divided

## Challenges in the Pancreatitis Patient

- Dissection can be **challenging** in patients with pancreatitis depending on the extent of surrounding inflammation
- The **transverse colon mesentery** may be fused to:
    - The anterior surface of the pancreas
    - The posterior surface of the stomach
- **Meticulous dissection** is needed to avoid:
    - Devascularization of the transverse colon
    - Injury to the stomach
    - Significant hemorrhage

## Identification of the Superior Mesenteric Vein (SMV)

- The **middle colic** and **gastroepiploic veins** are encountered toward the head of the pancreas
- These commonly join to form a **gastrocolic trunk**, which can be followed to the SMV
- **Ligation of the gastrocolic trunk** and other draining tributaries prevents unintentional traction injury and bleeding
- Careful dissection allows exposure of the SMV, which can be **traced to the inferior border of the pancreas**

## Control of SMV Bleeding

- Bleeding encountered during dissection of the gastroepiploic vein, gastrocolic trunk, or SMV can be controlled by:
    - Placing the **left hand behind the head of the pancreas/duodenum**
    - **Compressing the SMV/portal vein** between the thumb and left fingers
- A carefully placed **Prolene stitch** can typically control SMV bleeding
- **Specific attention** should be paid to avoid **narrowing or occluding the SMV**

## Distal Pancreas Dissection and Splenectomy

- The **retroperitoneal reflection** between the inferior border of the pancreas and transverse mesocolon is divided
- This mobilizes the **entire length of the gland** from the neck to the tail
- The **splenic flexure** is mobilized
- The **short gastric vessels** are ligated and divided
- The **peritoneal attachments to the spleen** are divided
- The **spleen** is mobilized medially out of the left upper quadrant
- Dissection continues to the level of the **takeoff of the splenic artery**

## Splenic Vessel Division

- The **splenic artery** is divided at its origin from the **celiac trunk**
- The **splenic vein** is divided at the level of the **portal vein**
- Depending on the location of the **inferior mesenteric vein**, this tributary may be spared
- The **coronary vein** can serve as an anatomic landmark coursing between the common hepatic and splenic arteries and frequently can be spared

## Splenic Preservation Options

- Splenic preservation can be considered, **particularly for benign disease**
- Two approaches:
    1. Dissection of the pancreatic tail out of the **splenic hilum** while preserving the **left gastroepiploic** and **short gastric vessels**
    2. The **splenic artery and vein may be preserved** and the posterior surface of the pancreas dissected off of these structures
- Splenic preservation avoids the long-term infectious risks of asplenism

## Portal Dissection — Overview

- Once the **infrapancreatic and splenic dissection** is completed, attention is turned to the **suprapancreatic dissection**
- **Cholecystectomy** is performed
- **Aberrant vascular anatomy** should be identified in advance on preoperative imaging
- The **gastrohepatic ligament** is opened widely

## Portal Dissection — Hepatic Artery and GDA

- The **station 8** (common hepatic artery lymph node) is usually a good marker of the hepatic artery
- The **common hepatic artery** is traced distally to identify the **right gastric artery**, which is divided between silk ties
- This typically exposes the **gastroduodenal artery (GDA)**
- The GDA is either **suture ligated** or divided with a **35 mm vascular stapler**

## Confirming Hepatic Inflow Before GDA Division

- Before division of the GDA:
    - The **left and right hepatic arteries** are identified
    - The GDA is **occluded with a bulldog or spoon clamp** to ensure hepatic inflow is not compromised
- This confirms:
    - The anatomy has been **correctly identified**
    - The GDA has **not been mistaken** for the proper or common hepatic artery
    - Hepatic inflow is **not dependent on retrograde flow** through the GDA from the SMA (as may occur in severe celiac stenosis)

## Aberrant Arterial Anatomy

- In cases of aberrant arterial anatomy with a **common hepatic trunk from the SMA**:
    - The common hepatic artery will travel **behind the pancreas** with the SMV
    - It will be visualized **posteriorly and to the left** of the GDA
- If this is the case:
    - It may be easier to identify the **proper hepatic artery and GDA**
    - Trace those structures **posteriorly** to the common hepatic artery
- Preoperative imaging is critical for identifying such variants

## Bile Duct Isolation and Division

- Division of the GDA reliably exposes the **portal vein** immediately posterior
- Dissection along the **anterior and medial border** of the bile duct continues
- The bile duct is **isolated with a vessel loop**
- Isolation is performed **from medial to lateral** to avoid inadvertent injury to the portal vein
- Careful attention is paid to ensure there is not a **replaced or accessory right hepatic artery** tracing behind and lateral to the bile duct

## Bile Duct Division — Malignant Indications

- The bile duct is **divided and sent for frozen** if the operation is for a malignant indication
- If a **stent** was placed preoperatively:
    - The stent is sent for **gross pathology**
    - The bile duct is **swabbed for culture**
- A **bulldog clamp** is placed on the proximal bile duct
- The handle is oriented **laterally** to avoid it interfering with the ongoing dissection

## Completion of the Portal Tunnel

- Once the portal dissection is complete, the **tunnel beneath the pancreas** connecting the **portal vein and SMV** is completed
- A **Penrose drain or umbilical tape** is used to assist with retraction
- This tunnel is a critical step connecting the superior and inferior dissection planes

::: callout-note
**Figure 117C.1**: A tunnel beneath the pancreas connecting the portal vein and SMV is completed and a Penrose drain or umbilical tape is used to assist with retraction.
:::

## Pancreatic Neck Division — Two-Specimen Approach

- Depending on the indication for total pancreatectomy, the **pancreatic neck may be divided** followed by dissection of the **uncinate process off the SMA** as is performed in PD
- This results in **two specimens**
- This is the **most commonly employed method** of total pancreatectomy
- It allows a familiar, stepwise approach combining PD and distal pancreatectomy techniques

## En Bloc Resection

- In cases where division of the pancreatic neck is **not appropriate**, the specimen may be resected **en bloc**
- En bloc resection can be **technically challenging**
- The safest and most efficient approach:
    - **Fully mobilize the entire specimen**
    - **Lift the left pancreas** out of the operative field to the patient's right side
    - Complete the **uncinate dissection** with the specimen elevated
- This provides excellent exposure of the retropancreatic portal vein and SMA

## Pylorus Preservation vs. Classic Total Pancreatectomy

- The **duodenum or stomach** is divided at the discretion of the surgeon
- There is some data to suggest **better nutritional outcomes and quality of life** in patients that undergo **pylorus-preserving total pancreatectomy** compared with classic total pancreatectomy
- The choice depends on the indication, disease extent, and surgeon preference

## Jejunal Resection

- The **jejunum** is divided approximately **10 cm distal to the ligament of Treitz**
- The **mesentery** is divided along the surface using an **energy device**
- The dissection should proceed **immediately adjacent to the jejunum** to avoid unintentional bleeding from the jejunal mesentery
- The **ligament of Treitz** is fully mobilized and the jejunum is passed through the defect

## Uncinate Resection — En Bloc Technique

- If the specimen is to be removed en bloc, the remaining uncinate dissection is best performed by **lifting the left pancreas out of the operative field toward the patient's right side**
- This exposes the **retropancreatic portal vein and SMA**
- **Extreme care** is taken to avoid avulsing the remaining **venous tributaries** to the portal vein
- These are divided with **clips, ties, or a 35 mm vascular stapler** as appropriate

## SMA Skeletonization

- Once the pancreatic head is fully mobilized off the portal vein, a **vein retractor** is used to apply gentle **leftward traction** on the portal vein
- This exposes the **SMA** nicely
- The SMA is **skeletonized** to free the remaining attachments to the **uncinate process and retroperitoneum**
- Branches are divided as appropriate using:
    - Energy device
    - Ties
    - Clips
    - 35 mm vascular stapler

## Specimen Removal and Hemostasis

- The **specimen is passed off the field**
- **Margins** are sent for frozen section as appropriate
- **Absolute hemostasis** is ensured
- The operative field is carefully inspected before proceeding to reconstruction

## Reconstruction — Overview

- A small defect is created in the **transverse mesocolon**, to the right of the **middle colic vessel**
- The **jejunal limb** is delivered into the upper abdomen
- The **staple line** is oversewn
- An **end-to-side hepaticojejunostomy** is created
- The biliary anastomosis is the key reconstruction step since there is no pancreatic anastomosis

## Hepaticojejunostomy — Dilated Bile Duct

- If the bile duct is **dilated**, a **running anastomosis** is created
- The **posterior layer** is fashioned with **PDS suture**
- The bowel is opened with **needle point electrocautery**
- A **second posterior layer** of interrupted **Vicryl sutures** is created to ensure the mucosa is appropriately incorporated
- The **anterior layer** is performed with a **second PDS suture**

## Hepaticojejunostomy — Small or Thin-Walled Duct

- If the bile duct is **small or particularly thin-walled**, an **interrupted anastomosis** is created
- Suture options:
    - **PDS sutures**
    - **Vicryl sutures**
- This technique allows more precise mucosa-to-mucosa approximation in delicate ducts

::: callout-note
**Figure 117C.3A**: Posterior wall biliary anastomosis.

**Figure 117C.3B**: Anterior wall biliary anastomosis.
:::

## Gastrojejunostomy / Duodenojejunostomy

- Approximately **30 cm downstream**, an **antecolic duodeno- or gastrojejunostomy** is created
- This is **handsewn with 2 layers of PDS**
- The jejunum is **tacked to the defect** in the right colon mesentery with interrupted silk sutures
- The defect at the **ligament of Treitz** is closed with silk sutures
- This restores gastrointestinal continuity

## Drains and Wound Management

- A **single 19-round Blake drain** is placed behind the biliary anastomosis
- **Hemostasis** is again ensured
- An **incisional wound vac** is frequently placed, especially in cases with prior instrumentation of the biliary tree
- The wound vac may help reduce surgical site infection risk in contaminated fields

## Minimally Invasive Total Pancreatectomy

- A handful of centers have reported acceptable outcomes with either a **laparoscopic** or **robotic** approach for total pancreatectomy
- Minimally invasive total pancreatectomy should be **limited to high-volume centers** with significant experience in minimally invasive pancreatic surgery
- The complexity of the operation demands advanced minimally invasive expertise

## Islet Cell Transplantation — History and Goals

- Total pancreatectomy with **islet auto transplantation** was first performed in **1977 at the University of Minnesota** for a patient with refractory chronic pancreatitis
- The goal of islet cell transplantation is to **prevent, or at least mitigate, the consequences of type III diabetes** by restoring beta cell function
- This is a critical adjunct for patients undergoing total pancreatectomy for benign disease

## Islet Cell Transplantation — Indications

- Generally accepted indications for total pancreatectomy with islet auto transplantation:
    - **Refractory chronic pancreatitis**
    - **Recurrent acute pancreatitis**
    - **Hereditary pancreatitis**
- Some centers have advocated for **expanded indications**, but this remains controversial
- Expanded indications should only be considered at **highly specialized centers**, ideally under an investigational protocol
- Either **pylorus preservation** or **antrectomy** is acceptable in most cases

## Islet Cell Transplantation — Islet Isolation

- After total pancreatectomy, the specimen is delivered to a **laboratory with experience in islet isolation**
- The **pancreatic duct is infused with collagenase**
- **Islets are harvested** from the digested tissue
- Depending on institutional resources and expertise, islets may be processed **on or off site**

## Islet Cell Transplantation — Portal Infusion

- Once available, islets are **infused into the portal circulation**:
    - During the **same operation**, or
    - **Percutaneously** as a staged procedure
- **Portal pressures** should be monitored closely and **not exceed 25 cm H₂O**
- Increased portal pressures during delivery increase the risk of **portal vein thrombosis**
- Careful monitoring is essential for safe islet delivery

## Completion Total Pancreatectomy — IPMN

- This continues to be an area of **significant debate**
- In the setting of **main-duct or multifocal IPMN**, the patient should be counseled preoperatively that this disease represents a **field defect** and the entire gland may be at risk
- Generally, the **morbidity of total pancreatectomy outweighs** that of prophylactic pancreatectomy
- Scenarios warranting total pancreatectomy in fit patients:
    - **Diffuse main duct involvement**
    - **Multifocal disease** in high-risk patients
    - **Persistent high-grade dysplasia** at the pancreatic resection margin

## Completion Total Pancreatectomy — IPMN Management Algorithm

- Frozen section is sent intraoperatively
- If the margin returns as **high-grade dysplasia**, an attempt is made to **clear this margin**
- If there is **persistent high-grade dysplasia** at the resection margin, **total pancreatectomy is performed** if there are no contraindications
- If the patient is **not appropriate** for total pancreatectomy, or there is **low-grade dysplasia** at the resection margin, **long-term surveillance** is the approach (as with all patients with IPMN)

## Completion Total Pancreatectomy — Adenocarcinoma

- **Pancreatic adenocarcinoma at the resection margin** is a poor prognostic indicator and likely a marker of **aggressive biology**
- When performing a Whipple for adenocarcinoma:
    - The **pancreatic neck margin** is sent for frozen section analysis
    - Every attempt is made to **clear this margin**
    - **Total pancreatectomy is avoided whenever possible**
- There is **conflicting evidence** as to whether frozen section analysis with clearance of the pancreatic neck margin is associated with improved survival
- Outcomes after total pancreatectomy for adenocarcinoma are **poor**, and this operation is **rarely indicated**, even in the setting of a positive resection margin after partial pancreatectomy

## Postoperative Care — Immediate

- Patient is monitored in the **intensive care unit overnight**
- Started on an **insulin drip**
- A **nasogastric tube** is typically left in place and removed on the morning of **postoperative day one**
- The **Foley catheter** is removed once it is no longer necessary for urine output monitoring

## Postoperative Care — Diet and Medications

- Patient is **slowly advanced to a diabetic diet** over the coming days
- **Endocrinology** assists with dosing of long- and short-acting insulin
- The **epidural catheter** is removed once the patient is tolerating a full liquid diet
- **Pancreatic enzymes** are administered as the patient begins to increase their oral intake
- The **surgical drain** is removed assuming it is nonbilious

## Postoperative Care — Discharge and Follow-Up

- **Nutrition and diabetes education is paramount**
- The patient is discharged home once all criteria are met
- The patient is evaluated **frequently as an outpatient** by:
    - Surgical team
    - Endocrinology team
    - Nutrition team
- Lifelong pancreatic enzyme replacement and insulin therapy are required
- Close multidisciplinary follow-up ensures optimal long-term outcomes

## Summary — Key Points

- Total pancreatectomy is a major operation with significant metabolic consequences
- **Careful patient selection** and extensive preoperative counseling are essential
- Best suited for **benign and premalignant disease** (chronic/recurrent pancreatitis, hereditary pancreatitis, diffuse IPMN)
- Rarely indicated for pancreatic adenocarcinoma due to poor outcomes
- The operation combines techniques of **pancreaticoduodenectomy** and **distal pancreatectomy**
- **Islet auto transplantation** should be considered for benign indications to mitigate brittle diabetes
- Reconstruction involves **hepaticojejunostomy** and **gastrojejunostomy/duodenojejunostomy**
- **Multidisciplinary care** (surgery, endocrinology, nutrition) is critical for long-term success
